prompts.SKILL_DISTILL:
You are writing ONE reusable capability card for a weaker terminal agent on
Terminal Bench V2.1. The card will be injected into a DIFFERENT TB21 task
from the same capability family, not the task below. The subtask SUCCEEDED:
the card is the procedure the weak model should follow when it faces the
same kind of subtask. A card that only works on this task is a failure.

SUBTASK LABEL: <label>
SUBTASK DESCRIPTION: <description>
STEPS OF THE SUBTASK:
<steps_view>
SEGMENT POSITION: <segment_position>

<profile_section>

Read the weak model profile FIRST. It is the capability boundary of your
reader: every node you write must be an action this exact model can carry
out as written. Where the profile names a weakness, add an explicit guard;
where it says the model cannot do something, never assume it can.

Work in five passes.

Pass 1 - abstract the capability.
Treat the steps as ONE instance of a reusable capability. Decide, for
yourself:
- capability: a short verb-and-object phrase that names the general skill
  (for example "recover a key from known plaintext-ciphertext pairs"). Do
  not use this task's name, file names, or specific tool names in this
  phrase.
- observable_trigger: the concrete signs a new TB21 task shows when this
  capability applies: file types, input structure, error text, available
  tools, required output. Tool names are allowed here.
- invariants: the steps that remain correct when the task's file names,
  constants, and tools change.
- variants: the choices that differ across tasks in this capability family.
  Name a variant type you recognize from the family even if only one variant
  appears in the steps view; but do not invent action steps for variants
  you did not observe.
- failure_guard: the weak reader's most likely failure here, taken from the
  profile.

If the segment fits none of the TB21 capability families below, use
"general terminal procedure" and write only the meta-rules you can support.

TB21 capability families:
- source build, install and verification
- runtime crash, hang and resource diagnosis
- environment and dependency setup
- numerical and scientific computation with result validation
- cryptographic analysis and security forensics
- sequence, primer and bioinformatics work
- distributed PyTorch and parallel execution
- data, text and large-file processing
- terminal interaction and recovery
- final verification and submission

Pass 2 - write the decision procedure.
Write 5 to 9 decision nodes. A node is one decision, not a script:
When <observable condition>, do <general action>; verify <pass signal>; if
it fails, <fallback>.
Use only the invariants. For each variant, add a short condition inside the
node ("if the task uses X, ...; otherwise ..."). Every action step must be
grounded in an observed action or observation from the steps view; omit a
step rather than invent it. Do not add separate TB21 discipline nodes;
instead weave the discipline into the verify and fallback parts of nodes:
check before acting, read the error before retrying, run the verifier before
calling mark_task_complete.

Pass 3 - make it executable for the weak model.
- one action per node, imperative voice, no self-numbering;
- every task-specific value is a <placeholder> in angle brackets: file
  names, paths, commands, flags, API names, constants, error strings,
  entities;
- a command may appear only in a general form that works after substituting
  the placeholders;
- scripts used as tools: write only the invocation pattern, the inputs, and
  the expected output—never include the script body, even if the trajectory
  showed it in full;
- code as the deliverable (when the task is to write a program or module):
  describe the structure the code must satisfy and how to verify it with
  the task's tests—do not include the implementation;
- no code block longer than three lines;
- keep the whole card between 1,500 and 2,500 characters; if 5 to 9 full
  nodes do not fit in 2,500 characters, prefer fewer well-written nodes
  over many truncated ones.

Pass 4 - write the trigger and the summary.
The reader does not see this card at first. It sees a list with one line
per card: the summary, then the when_to_use text. From that one line it
decides whether to open the card. So the line must say WHAT the card
teaches and WHEN to open it.

First choose the ONE moment in a new task when the reader should open
this card, and start when_to_use with its phrase, copied exactly:
  "At task start,"
      the reader has just received the task and is reading the task
      description and the given files;
  "After the first environment check,"
      the reader has run its first ls, which, import or network probe and
      now knows what is installed and what is reachable;
  "When a command fails, hangs, or repeats,"
      a command gave an error, got stuck, or the same action keeps
      repeating without progress;
  "Before submitting,"
      the work looks done and the reader is about to run the final check
      and submit;
  "At any step,"
      a basic rule that holds at every step. Use this only when none of
      the four moments above fits.
SEGMENT POSITION is a hint, not a rule: an early segment often belongs
"At task start," or "After the first environment check,"; the last
segment often belongs "Before submitting,".

Then write:
- summary: one sentence, a verb and an object, saying what the card
  teaches. Do not put the trigger in the summary. No task or
  subtask names.
- when_to_use: the timing phrase, then the signs the reader can see at
  that moment (file types, input structure, error text, available tools,
  required output), and the preconditions. One or two sentences.
- not_applicable_when: the signs that this card is wrong for the task.
  Keep these out of when_to_use.

Length: summary and when_to_use together should stay under about 400
characters and must never go over 1,000. Write only complete sentences.
If the text is too long, drop details; never cut a sentence off. Do not
make it vague to make it short: the reader must still be able to tell
this card apart from the other cards in the same list.

Pass 5 - transfer audit.
Before output, check every item; if any fails, rewrite the card:
1. Replace the task's language, tools, file names and constants in your
   mind. Do the nodes still make sense?
2. Is the trigger observable from the task, not from its name?
3. Is every task-specific token a <placeholder>?
4. Are there 5 to 9 decision nodes and 1,500 to 2,500 characters?
5. Does when_to_use start with exactly one of the five timing phrases?
6. Is the summary free of the trigger, and are summary and when_to_use
   complete sentences, together under 1,000 characters (about 400 is
   best)?

Output ONLY JSON with exactly these fields:
{"when_to_use": "<timing phrase, then the observable trigger and the
preconditions, in one or two sentences>",
  "steps": ["<one decision node: condition, action, verify, fallback>", ...],
  "not_applicable_when": "<observable conditions under which this card is
wrong>",
  "summary": "<one sentence: the reusable capability this card teaches
  (verb + object); no trigger, no task or subtask names>"}
prompts.SKILL_DIAGNOSE:
You are writing ONE reusable capability card for a weaker terminal agent on
Terminal Bench V2.1, from a subtask where it went wrong. The card will be
injected into a DIFFERENT TB21 task from the same capability family. Teach
the reader to recognize a general failure pattern and follow a corrective
procedure; do not write a fix for this task.

SUBTASK LABEL: <label>
SUBTASK DESCRIPTION: <description>
WHAT THE PRECEDING PART OF THE TRAJECTORY WAS DOING:
<context_summary>
STEPS OF THE SUBTASK:
<steps_view>
SEGMENT POSITION: <segment_position>

<profile_section>

Read the weak model profile FIRST. It is the capability boundary of your
reader: every node you write must be an action this exact model can carry
out as written. Where the profile names a weakness that caused or worsened
this failure, the guard must address it.

Work in five passes.

Pass 1 - diagnose the general failure pattern.
Find the step or decision where the weak model went wrong. Name the pattern
at the reader's level: skipped verification, misread observation, wrong
tool, unread error before retry, wrong order, early success claim, or an
unrecognized precondition. Do not write "logical error" or this task's name.
Use the context summary only to understand what the reader was trying to do.

Pass 2 - abstract the capability.
Decide, for yourself:
- capability: a short verb-and-object phrase that names the general skill.
  Do not use this task's name, file names, or specific tool names in this
  phrase.
- observable_trigger: the signs a new TB21 task shows when this pattern can
  occur (file types, input structure, error text, tool state, required
  output). Tool names are allowed here.
- invariants: the corrective steps that hold across tasks.
- variants: the choices that differ across tasks. Name a variant type you
  recognize from the family even if only one variant appears in the steps
  view; but do not invent action steps for variants you did not observe.
- failure_guard: the guard that prevents this pattern from recurring.
- corrective_steps: the correct actions that the trajectory shows working,
  OR—where the trajectory only shows the mistake—the minimal corrective
  action the profile tells you the reader can execute (for example: read the
  error message before retrying). Do not invent multi-step procedures that
  are not grounded in the steps view or the failure pattern.

If the segment fits none of the TB21 capability families below, use
"general terminal procedure" and write only the meta-rules you can support.

TB21 capability families:
- source build, install and verification
- runtime crash, hang and resource diagnosis
- environment and dependency setup
- numerical and scientific computation with result validation
- cryptographic analysis and security forensics
- sequence, primer and bioinformatics work
- distributed PyTorch and parallel execution
- data, text and large-file processing
- terminal interaction and recovery
- final verification and submission

Pass 3 - write the corrective decision procedure.
Write 5 to 9 decision nodes. A node is one decision, not a script:
When <observable condition>, do <general action>; verify <pass signal>; if
it fails, <fallback>.
Use only the invariants. For each variant, add a short condition inside the
node ("if the task uses X, ...; otherwise ..."). The procedure must teach
the reader to recognize the failing behavior from observable signs, not from
this task's names.
For nodes where the trajectory only shows what went wrong and not what is
correct: write one node that detects the failure sign and one node that
names the corrective action from the profile or the failure pattern—do not
invent a multi-step procedure beyond what the evidence supports.
Do not add separate TB21 discipline nodes; instead weave the discipline into
the verify and fallback parts of nodes: check before acting, read the error
before retrying, run the verifier before calling mark_task_complete.

Make it executable for the weak model:
- one action per node, imperative voice, no self-numbering;
- every task-specific value is a <placeholder> in angle brackets: file
  names, paths, commands, flags, API names, constants, error strings,
  entities;
- a command may appear only in a general form that works after substituting
  the placeholders;
- scripts used as tools: write only the invocation pattern, the inputs, and
  the expected output—never include the script body, even if the trajectory
  showed it in full;
- code as the deliverable (when the task is to write a program or module):
  describe the structure the code must satisfy and how to verify it with
  the task's tests—do not include the implementation;
- no code block longer than three lines;
- keep the whole card between 1,500 and 2,500 characters; if 5 to 9 full
  nodes do not fit in 2,500 characters, prefer fewer well-written nodes
  over many truncated ones.

Pass 4 - write the trigger and the summary.
The reader does not see this card at first. It sees a list with one line
per card: the summary, then the when_to_use text. From that one line it
decides whether to open the card. So the line must say WHAT the card
teaches and WHEN to open it.

First choose the ONE moment in a new task when the reader should open
this card, and start when_to_use with its phrase, copied exactly:
  "At task start,"
      the reader has just received the task and is reading the task
      description and the given files;
  "After the first environment check,"
      the reader has run its first ls, which, import or network probe and
      now knows what is installed and what is reachable;
  "When a command fails, hangs, or repeats,"
      a command gave an error, got stuck, or the same action keeps
      repeating without progress;
  "Before submitting,"
      the work looks done and the reader is about to run the final check
      and submit;
  "At any step,"
      a basic rule that holds at every step. Use this only when none of
      the four moments above fits.
SEGMENT POSITION is a hint, not a rule: a failed segment often belongs
"When a command fails, hangs, or repeats,"; an early segment often
belongs "At task start," or "After the first environment check,"; the
last segment often belongs "Before submitting,".

Then write:
- summary: one sentence, a verb and an object, saying what the card
  teaches and the failure pattern it prevents. Do not put the trigger in
  the summary. No task or subtask names.
- when_to_use: the timing phrase, then the signs the reader can see at
  that moment (file types, input structure, error text, available tools,
  required output), and the failing behavior to recognize. One or two
  sentences.
- not_applicable_when: the signs that this card is wrong for the task.
  Keep these out of when_to_use.

Length: summary and when_to_use together should stay under about 400
characters and must never go over 1,000. Write only complete sentences.
If the text is too long, drop details; never cut a sentence off. Do not
make it vague to make it short: the reader must still be able to tell
this card apart from the other cards in the same list.

Pass 5 - transfer audit.
Before output, check every item; if any fails, rewrite the card:
1. Replace the task's language, tools, file names and constants in your
   mind. Do the nodes still make sense?
2. Is the trigger observable from the task, not from its name?
3. Is every task-specific token a <placeholder>?
4. Are there 5 to 9 decision nodes and 1,500 to 2,500 characters?
5. Does when_to_use start with exactly one of the five timing phrases?
6. Is the summary free of the trigger, and are summary and when_to_use
   complete sentences, together under 1,000 characters (about 400 is
   best)?

Output ONLY JSON with exactly these fields:
{"when_to_use": "<timing phrase, then the observable trigger and the
failing behavior to recognize, in one or two sentences>",
  "steps": ["<one decision node: condition, action, verify, fallback>", ...],
  "not_applicable_when": "<observable conditions under which this card is
wrong>",
  "summary": "<one sentence: what the card teaches instead (verb + object)
and the failure pattern it prevents; no trigger, no task or subtask names>"}
prompts.REWRITE:
A skill written for a weak model failed its acceptance exam. Rewrite it
only if the failure reveals a general defect. This is a Terminal Bench V2.1
skill; the card will be used on other tasks, so task-specific details must
not enter it.

SKILL (current version):
<skill_text>

EXAM QUESTION:
<question_text>

REAL SITUATION THE EXAM WAS CUT FROM (the trajectory the skill was
learned from; use it to see what the skill must really cover):
<source_context>

WEAK MODEL'S ANSWER:
<weak_answer>

WHAT WAS WRONG WITH THE ANSWER:
<error_description>

<profile_section>

<scope_section>No reference answer is available to you, and you must not invent or guess
one.

Work in three steps:

1. Classify why the weak model did not succeed. Choose exactly one category:
   - "misread": the weak model misunderstood the instruction;
   - "missing_step": the skill skipped an intermediate step that needed to
     be spelled out;
   - "wrong_trigger": the condition for when to apply the skill was unclear,
     so the weak model applied it wrongly or at the wrong moment;
   - "other": none of the above.

2. Decide whether the failure is a general defect in the skill or a
   task-specific issue.
   - General defect: a missing intermediate step, a trigger the reader
     cannot observe, a step the reader cannot execute, or a misleading
     order. Rewrite the skill.
   - Task-specific issue: a fact about this exam's files, values, tools or
     expected answer. Do not encode it. Return the skill unchanged and say
     in rewrite_reason that the failure is task-specific.

3. If you rewrite, keep the three bracket sections of the original skill
   ([When to use]/[Steps]/[Do not use when]): rewrite each
   section's content, never collapse them into prose. Reproduce
   the bracketed section headers exactly as written, each on its own line.
   Change the wording, granularity, or trigger conditions of the skill --
   not its underlying idea.
   Rewrite to 5 to 9 decision nodes and 1,500 to 2,500 characters. Compress
   instead of appending. Every node must remain a general decision rule;
   task-specific values become <placeholders>. A script may appear only as
   its input, output, and invocation; never include its implementation, and
   never use a code block longer than three lines.
   Then write a fresh capability-level summary of the REWRITTEN skill: the
   reusable capability it teaches (verb + object) and its observable
   trigger, with no task or subtask names. Keep it on one line.

Hard constraint: do NOT copy specific values, file names, entities, or any
other concrete details from the exam question into the skill. The rewritten
skill must stay general; it must not smuggle in the answer to this
particular exam.

Transfer audit before output:
1. Would the rewritten nodes still make sense if the exam's language, tools,
   file names and constants changed?
2. Is every trigger observable from the task, not from its name?
3. Is every task-specific token a <placeholder>?
4. Are there 5 to 9 decision nodes and 1,500 to 2,500 characters?
If any check fails, rewrite again.

Output ONLY JSON with exactly these fields:
{"failure_category": "<misread|missing_step|wrong_trigger|other>",
  "skill_text": "<the rewritten skill, plain text>",
  "rewrite_reason": "<one or two sentences: what you changed and why, or why
  the failure is task-specific and the skill is unchanged>",
  "summary": "<one line: the reusable capability the rewritten skill teaches
  (verb + object) and its observable trigger; no task or subtask names>"}
prompts.SEGMENT:
You are given the view of one agent trajectory from Terminal Bench V2.1.
Split it into capability-coherent sub-procedures.

TRAJECTORY:
<trajectory_view>

A segment is one reusable sub-procedure, not one task-specific step. A good
segment has:
- an observable trigger: the situation where the sub-procedure starts;
- a general goal: what it achieves, stated without this task's names or
  concrete values;
- a boundary: the point where the next sub-procedure begins.

Split the trajectory into at most <K> such subtasks.

Rules:
- The segments must cover the whole trajectory in order, without gaps and
  without overlaps: the first segment starts at step 0, the last one ends at
  the final step, and consecutive segments touch (the end index of one is
  the start index of the next; end indices are exclusive). Every step must
  belong to exactly one segment.
- Use at most <K> segments, and every segment must contain at least one step.
- Merge adjacent steps that belong to the same capability. Environment
  setup, one-off commands, and task-specific data wrangling should be folded
  into the nearest capability segment, not given their own segment; their
  steps still belong to a segment (so coverage stays complete), but the
  segment's label and description name the capability, not the setup.
- If the natural capability boundaries number more than <K>, merge the most
  closely related segments first; prefer folding setup or discovery steps
  into a real capability segment over merging two distinct capabilities.
- Do not restate the content of the steps. Describe each segment at the
  level of its observable trigger and general goal, so the step content and
  the segment description stay separate.
- "label" is a short capability phrase, not a task-specific phrase (for
  example "build and verify a source project", "recover a key from known
  pairs").
- "description" is one or two sentences that name the observable trigger and
  the general goal.
- "success" says whether that segment's own goal was achieved by the end of
  the segment, independent of whether the overall trajectory succeeded.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per segment in order, with exactly
these fields:
[
  {"start": <first step index, integer>,
    "end": <step index after the last step of this segment, exclusive, integer>,
    "label": "<short capability phrase>",
    "description": "<one or two sentences: observable trigger and general goal>",
    "success": <true or false>}
]
Return no text before or after the JSON array.
prompts.CLUSTER_TRIGGER_FAMILY:
You classify ONE segment of a terminal-agent trajectory into the trigger
timing at which a reusable skill distilled from it should be opened.

SEGMENT LABEL: <label>
SEGMENT DESCRIPTION: <description>
SEGMENT SOURCE: <source>
SEGMENT SUCCESS: <success>
SEGMENT POSITION: <segment_position>
STEPS:
<steps_view>

Choose exactly ONE family key from this closed list:

- "at_task_start": the reader has just received a new task and is reading
  the task description, inputs and initial files.
- "after_first_environment_check": the reader has run its first ls, which,
  import or network probe and now knows what is installed and reachable.
- "when_command_fails": a command produced an error, hung, or the same
  action keeps repeating without progress.
- "before_submitting": the work looks done and the reader is about to run
  the final verifier and submit.
- "at_any_step": a basic rule that applies at every step and fits none of
  the four moments above.

Use the segment position only as a hint: an early segment often belongs to
the first two families, and the last segment often belongs to
"before_submitting". Judge from the observed steps, not the task name.

Output ONLY JSON with exactly these fields:
{"family": "<one of the five keys above>",
  "reason": "<one short sentence naming the observable cue>"}
prompts.CLUSTER_SUBTASKS:
You group subtasks of ONE trigger-timing family by the problem they
handle. The reader of the resulting skills is a weaker terminal agent on
Terminal Bench V2.1. Group subtasks that call for the same reusable
capability, even when their task names, files and tools differ.

FAMILY: <family>
FAMILY MEANING: <family_definition>

SUBTASK CARDS:
<cards>

Rules:
- Use every SUBTASK_ID from the cards exactly once.
- Never invent a SUBTASK_ID and never repeat one.
- A group may have one member when no other card belongs with it.
- The theme must name a capability (a verb and an object), not a task name.
- The reason must state what the members have in common.

Output ONLY JSON with exactly this shape:
{"clusters": [
  {"theme": "<capability theme>",
    "subtask_ids": ["<exact SUBTASK_ID from the cards>", "..."],
    "reason": "<one sentence: what the members have in common>"}
]}

prompts.TRIAL_FAILURE_ANALYSIS:
You analyze ONE failed trial of a weaker terminal agent on Terminal Bench
V2.1. The trial is selected only because its acceptance verdict is failure.
Your job is diagnosis, not action selection.

TASK INSTRUCTION:
<task_instruction>

TRIAL STEPS:
<trial_steps>

SKILLS ACTUALLY DELIVERED TO THIS TRIAL:
<available_skills>

ALL SKILLS IN THE CURRENT BANK:
<all_skills>

Read the trial first, then the delivered skills. Decide why the trial failed
and write the answer in ordinary prose. Do not force the cause into a fixed
category. Distinguish, when the evidence supports it:

- the model read a relevant, correct skill and still failed because of its
  own terminal behavior, planning, speed, or comprehension limits;
- a relevant skill existed but the model never opened or applied it;
- the model opened a skill but the skill's trigger, steps, or guard was
  wrong or incomplete;
- no skill in the bank addresses this failure, so a new capability is
  needed.

Before writing the reason, check every skill under SKILLS ACTUALLY DELIVERED.
If a delivered skill matched the situation but was not opened, or was opened
but not followed, include it in `skills` with the concrete issue. Do not omit
a relevant delivered skill from that list.

Use only evidence visible in the steps and skills. If the cause is unclear,
say what is unclear instead of inventing certainty.

Output ONLY JSON:
{"reason": "<a clear paragraph explaining the failure>",
  "profile_note": "<what this says about the model as a student, or an empty string>",
  "skills": [
    {"skill_id": "<exact bank skill id or empty string>",
      "issue": "<what this skill did or failed to do>",
      "step_start": <the 0-based step where this skill should have been
                     opened, or where its guidance went wrong; for a skill
                     the model never opened, use the step where the failure
                     first became visible>,
      "step_end": <exclusive end step>}
  ],
  "new_skill_note": "<what new capability is missing, or an empty string>"}
prompts.TRIAL_EXAM_ANALYSIS:
You analyze ONE failed paper exam of a weaker terminal agent on Terminal
Bench V2.1. Your job is diagnosis, not action selection.

How the exam works: the scene below was cut from a real task at one point in
time. The examined model saw only the scene and the skill catalog, chose up to
a few skills to open, read them, and wrote a plan for what to do from this
point. Nothing was executed. A plan in prose with no command output is the
required answer format, so never give "the model did not execute commands"
or "the trial stopped after a plan" as a cause. A judge compared the plan with
the expected behavior and marked it failed for the reason given below.

SCENE:
<scene_text>

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR (the grading standard the judge used):
<expected_behavior>

JUDGE'S REASON FOR THE FAILURE:
<judge_reason>

SKILL UNDER EXAMINATION (this exam was written for it):
SKILL_ID: <exam_skill_id>
<exam_skill_content>

SKILL CATALOG (exactly what the examined model saw when choosing):
<skill_catalog>

SKILLS THE MODEL OPENED:
<opened_skills>

THE MODEL'S PLAN:
<plan>

Explain the defect the judge named. Take the judge's reason as the fact to
explain; if the scene itself contradicts it, say so plainly.

Only the stage this scene is about matters. A skill meant for an earlier or
later stage is not applicable here, so not opening it is never a defect.

For the skill under examination, decide which of these holds:
- it was not opened, and its catalog line should have matched this scene:
  its trigger or description is defective;
- it was not opened, and its catalog line rightly does not match this
  scene: the model chose wrongly, or the scene is outside the skill's stage;
- it was opened, and it covers what the judge says is missing or wrong:
  the model did not follow a correct skill (a model limitation);
- it was opened, and it does not cover the defect, or it misleads: its
  content is defective.

List other skills only when they apply to this scene and contributed to the
failure (opened and misleading, or matching but not opened).

Use only evidence visible above. If the cause is unclear, say what is
unclear instead of inventing certainty.

Output ONLY JSON:
{"reason": "<a clear paragraph explaining the failure>",
  "exam_skill_issue": "<which case above holds for the skill under examination, and the concrete evidence>",
  "profile_note": "<what this says about the model as a student, or an empty string>",
  "skills": [
    {"skill_id": "<exact bank skill id of another applicable skill>",
      "issue": "<what this skill did or failed to do in this scene>"}
  ],

prompts.EXAM_SCENE:
Reconstruct one exam scene from a real trajectory. The scene is the
situation a reader faces when it reaches one cut point of the trajectory; the
reader will have to decide what to do next without seeing the steps below or
the skill that was written from them.

TASK INSTRUCTION (what the agent that produced the trajectory was asked to do):
<task_instruction>

STEPS BEFORE THE CUT (the real prefix; the reader sees everything up to here):
<prior_steps>

STEPS AFTER THE CUT (what actually happened next; ground the expected behavior
in these):
<future_steps>

THE SKILL UNDER EXAMINATION (its full text; use it only to understand what a
correct reader must notice and do):
<skill_content>

WHY THIS SKILL WAS WRITTEN OR CHANGED:
<change_note>

Write three fields, all in natural language:

- scene_text: the situation at the cut point, self-contained. Describe the
  task, the state reached so far, and the observations that matter, so a reader
  who never saw the trajectory can decide what to do next. End at the cut:
  never include the action or the observations that come after it.
- expected_behavior: what a reader who understands the situation should do
  next, and what it should verify. Say the behavior generally; it is the
  grading standard for a plan, not this trajectory's command lines.
- reference_answer: the best answer to the scene: the right action, in what
  order, and why. This is a grading reference and is never shown to the
  examined reader.

Hard rules:
- scene_text must NOT name or allude to any skill, the skill catalog, a skill
  file, or the fact that this scene comes from an exam or a trajectory.
- Use natural language throughout: no step indices, no ids, no bookkeeping
  fields. Concrete observations and values from the trajectory are allowed.
- Do not ask the reader a question; state the situation.

Output ONLY JSON with exactly these fields:
{"scene_text": "<the self-contained situation at the cut point>",
  "expected_behavior": "<what a correct reader should do next and verify>",
  "reference_answer": "<the right action, order, and why>"}

prompts.MERGE:

general form; do not paste the sources' sections one after another.

<profile_section>

MERGE MODE: <mode>
- "dedup": the skills teach the same thing. Distill them into one general
  lesson. Where the sources describe the same situation with task-specific
  details (task names, specific error messages, file names, values), write one
  general trigger and general steps that cover all of them. Do not center the
  skill on any single source's scenario.
- "conflict": the skills give opposite advice for the same situation. First
  work out why they conflict: which condition makes one course of action right
  and the other wrong. Then write one skill that states those conditions
  explicitly, so the reader can decide when to follow which course of action.

<skills_block>

Rules:
- Keep every distinct piece of advice from the sources, stated in general form.
- You may generalize the sources' conditions and steps; do not add advice that
  none of the sources supports.
- The merged skill carries the three bracketed sections every source skill
  carries: [When to use], [Steps], [Do not use when]. Reproduce
  the bracketed section headers exactly as written, each on its own line.
- Keep the weak-model-friendly style: short sentences, one instruction per
  sentence, explicit order, concrete trigger conditions.

Also write a one-line summary of the merged skill: what it is and does, in
one or two sentences. It will be shown as the skill's single line in a
directory of skills, so make it concrete and specific, and keep it on one

prompts.SIMILARITY:

no_weak_profile_section: No weak-model profile is provided. Treat the reader as a generally capable terminal agent: every step must be a concrete action it can carry out, one action per step. Do not assume any specific weakness.

trigger_families.before_submitting: the work looks done and the reader is about to run the final verifier and submit
trigger_families.at_any_step: a basic rule that applies at every step and fits none of the four moments above
